newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe says FIS should not run in Algerian poll.
newsitem.headline: Juppe says FIS should not run in Algerian poll.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on Monday Algeria's proposed parliamentary elections should be open to all legal democratic parties but not the outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).
"The only party we support in Algeria is the party of democracy...Legal political groups must take part in this election," he told France Inter radio in an interview.
But asked whether the FIS was among democratic parties, he said: "As long as you use bombs, car bombs and knives you are not a party backing democratic values."
The French government later announced it was naming a new ambassador to Algiers.

It said Alfred Siefer-Gaillard, who has been ambassador to Ottawa since April 1992, would represent Paris in Algiers, replacing Michel Leveque, recently named prime minister of Monaco. The principality selects its cabinet members from a list proposed by Paris.
Juppe voiced horror at worsening violence in Algeria, a former French colony, and compassion for its population, adding that France had no desire to interfere in Algerian affairs.
Former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing drew angry charges of interference from Algiers last week by calling for Islamists to be allowed to take part in the election.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette telephoned his Algerian colleague Ahmed Attaf on Sunday to try to defuse a row over whether Paris was meddling in the North African country where civil strife has claimed 60,000 lives in five years.
He told Attaf that France's official policy of non-interference in Algeria had not changed, a French ministry statement said.

De Charette also said he would adopt the principles that Attaf wanted to guide Franco-Algerian relations -- "mutual respect based on non-interference, a balance of interests and coordination on matters of mutual interest," it said.

French Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin has urged France to consult its European partners on a joint initiative, saying no one dared to discuss the conflict while Paris stayed silent about Algeria, which won independence from France in 1962 after a bloody war.
Violence flared in Algeria after authorities cancelled a 1992 election which the FIS was poised to win.
